manifests.title: Directed-angle animation with positive and negative arrows
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: To reduce an angle, add or subtract complete revolutions until the value lies in the desired interval. The operation changes the accumulated rotation but preserves the terminal side because every full revolution returns the ray to its prior direction. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Represent rotations in standard position and generate all coterminal angles.

manifests.title: Terminal-side family showing theta+360k degrees
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for directed rotation and coterminal angles.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Represent rotations in standard position and generate all coterminal angles.

manifests.title: Common error panel contrasting angle size with terminal-side location
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to confuse the magnitude of rotation with the terminal-side location. An angle of 765 degrees is not “the same angle” as 45 degrees in every sense; it is coterminal with it leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Represent rotations in standard position and generate all coterminal angles.

manifests.title: One revolution partitioned into degrees
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: Degree-minute-second notation is a base-60 place-value system. To convert to decimal degrees, divide minutes by 60 and seconds by 3600. To reverse the conversion, separate the whole degrees and repeatedly multiply the fractional part by 60. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Use degrees, revolutions, and degree-minute-second notation to measure and compare rotation.

manifests.title: Degree-minute-second place-value diagram
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for degree measure and angular coordinates.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Use degrees, revolutions, and degree-minute-second notation to measure and compare rotation.

manifests.title: Heading circle with clockwise navigation convention
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to treat 18 degrees 30 minutes as 18.30 degrees. Thirty minutes is one-half degree, so the correct decimal is 18.5 degrees leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Use degrees, revolutions, and degree-minute-second notation to measure and compare rotation.

manifests.title: Two different circles with equal s/r ratio
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: Radians convert circular geometry into ordinary real-number input. On the unit circle, radius one makes the numerical angle equal to signed arc length. This is why radians are the natural input for trigonometric functions and later Calculus formulas. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define radian measure as signed arc length divided by radius and explain why it is independent of circle size.

manifests.title: Real-number line wrapping onto a circle
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for radian measure as normalized arc length.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define radian measure as signed arc length divided by radius and explain why it is independent of circle size.

manifests.title: Degree-radian conversion wheel based on 2pi=360 degrees
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to regard pi as a unit attached to every radian angle. Pi appears in many exact conversions because a full revolution is 2pi, but an angle such as 2.4 radians need not contain pi leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define radian measure as signed arc length divided by radius and explain why it is independent of circle size.

manifests.title: Sector with radius, arc, and angle labels
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: The radian formulas work without an extra conversion factor because the radian definition already incorporates the circumference-to-radius relationship. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Derive and use s=r theta and A=(1/2)r^2 theta for angles measured in radians.

manifests.title: Derivation from fraction of full circumference and area
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for arc length and sector area.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Derive and use s=r theta and A=(1/2)r^2 theta for angles measured in radians.

manifests.title: Error panel showing why degree inputs need conversion
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to use s=r theta with degree input, producing an answer too large by a factor of 180/pi leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Derive and use s=r theta and A=(1/2)r^2 theta for angles measured in radians.

manifests.title: Rotating disk with equal angular but different linear speeds
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: The formula follows from s=r theta: divide both sides by elapsed time to obtain s/t=r(theta/t). In a belt or no-slip contact, connected rims share tangential speed even when their radii and angular speeds differ. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Relate angular speed, radius, and tangential speed using v=r omega.

manifests.title: Unit-conversion pipeline from rpm to rad/s
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for angular speed and linear speed.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Relate angular speed, radius, and tangential speed using v=r omega.

manifests.title: Pulley-belt diagram with equal tangential speed
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to assume all points on a rotating disk have the same linear speed because they complete a revolution together leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Relate angular speed, radius, and tangential speed using v=r omega.

manifests.title: Real-line strip wrapped around a circle
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: Positive t moves counterclockwise and negative t moves clockwise. Reducing t modulo 2pi identifies a convenient coterminal input without changing the terminal point. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Map any real number t to the unit-circle point reached by signed arc length t.

manifests.title: Multiple real inputs connected to one terminal point
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for wrapping the real line around the unit circle.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Map any real number t to the unit-circle point reached by signed arc length t.

manifests.title: Signed motion with clockwise and counterclockwise travel
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to treat the reduced angle as the only valid input rather than one representative of an infinite coterminal family leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Map any real number t to the unit-circle point reached by signed arc length t.

manifests.title: Unit-circle point with coordinate projections
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: A known coordinate immediately gives sine and cosine. If one coordinate is known, use the unit-circle equation to find the other, then use the quadrant to choose the correct sign. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define cosine and sine as the x- and y-coordinates of the unit-circle point P(t).

manifests.title: Coordinate signs by quadrant
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for sine and cosine as coordinate functions.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define cosine and sine as the x- and y-coordinates of the unit-circle point P(t).

manifests.title: Domain-range diagram for sine and cosine
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to reverse sine and cosine coordinates or to choose both coordinate signs without using quadrant information leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define cosine and sine as the x- and y-coordinates of the unit-circle point P(t).

manifests.title: Special-triangle derivations inside the unit circle
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: Once first-quadrant coordinates are derived, reflection symmetry places the same magnitudes in every quadrant with signs determined by coordinate location. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Derive exact unit-circle values from 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles.

manifests.title: Exact-value symmetry map
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for exact values from special triangles.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Derive exact unit-circle values from 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles.

manifests.title: Blank unit circle rebuilt from geometric anchors
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to swap the coordinates at pi/6 and pi/3 or to rationalize one tangent value inconsistently leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Derive exact unit-circle values from 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles.

manifests.title: Original angle, terminal side, and reference triangle
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: Reduce the angle if needed, identify the quadrant, find the acute distance to the nearest x-axis, evaluate the special-angle magnitude, and assign signs from the coordinate quadrant. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Use reference angles and quadrant signs to evaluate trigonometric functions of arbitrary rotations.

manifests.title: Quadrant sign chart derived from coordinates
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for reference angles, quadrants, and signs.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Use reference angles and quadrant signs to evaluate trigonometric functions of arbitrary rotations.

manifests.title: Error panel separating coterminal angle from reference angle
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why reference angles make exact evaluation possible for large, negative, and multi-revolution inputs leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Use reference angles and quadrant signs to evaluate trigonometric functions of arbitrary rotations.

manifests.title: Six-function ratio web
manifests.description: Follow the foundation example from its given information to the conclusion. The labels identify the mathematical feature that makes the result valid: The unit-circle identity produces two more identities by division: 1+tan^2 t=sec^2 t and cot^2 t+1=csc^2 t. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant from sine and cosine and state domains, signs, periods, and identities.

manifests.title: Pythagorean identity derivation by division
manifests.description: Read the numbered reasoning path in order. Each stage preserves the quantities, restrictions, or structural conditions needed for tangent and the reciprocal functions.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant from sine and cosine and state domains, signs, periods, and identities.

manifests.title: Domain-exclusion unit circle with zero coordinates marked
manifests.description: Compare the valid path with the tempting shortcut. The figure shows why to invert an angle or to write tan t as cos/sin leads to a false conclusion.
manifests.learnerOutcome: Define tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant from sine and cosine and state domains, signs, periods, and identities.
